title: Rome defines faith absolutely (living and dead); Reformed define the living add-on
source_text: LIII. Verum observandum est scopum Doctorum Ecclesiae Romanae hic esse fidem definire, prout absolute & in se consideratur, & eam tradere fidei definitionem quae non soli fidei vivae, sed etiam mortuae competat. Quo respectu nemo inter Reformatos fidem ab eis recte definiri negabit. Etenim dum illi fidem simpliciter definiunt, & prout est genus ad fidem historicam atque justificantem, eadem omnino definitione utuntur. Reformati vero dum fidem justificantem definiunt, definitione sua plerunque solum includere intendunt quod fides viva atque justificans fidei generatim consideratae superaddit.
pass_a_gloss: But it must be observed that the aim of the Doctors of the Roman Church here is to define faith as it is considered absolutely and in itself, and to hand down a definition of faith that belongs not only to living faith but also to dead. In which respect no one among the Reformed will deny that faith is rightly defined by them. For when they define faith simply, and as it is the genus for historic and justifying faith, they use altogether the same definition. But the Reformed, when they define justifying faith, by their definition for the most part intend to include only what living and justifying faith superadds to faith considered generally.
pass_b_english: Rome scopes the definition to absolute faith common to living and dead — a definition Reformed also use for faith as genus.
Reformed justifying-faith definitions mostly name only what living faith adds beyond faith in general.

lemmas.gloss: is considered absolutely and in itself

lemmas.latin: genus ad fidem historicam atque justificantem
lemmas.gloss: genus toward historic and justifying faith
